Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The Houston Rockets have looked like one of the best teams in the NBA through the first few games of the 2026-27 season. Their hot start to the new campaign continued on Monday, as they rode a strong night from Alperen Sengun to defeat the Atlanta Hawks for the second straight time, taking a 120-110 victory at home. Sengun had his way with the Hawks’ overmatched frontline. He put up 29 points, nine rebounds, and nine assists, and he also was his peak disruptive self on defense, adding six thefts as well to what was already such a stacked stat line. By putting up that kind of performance in the Rockets’ latest win, he joined Nikola Jokic as the only centers in NBA history to reach those numbers in a single game, according to StatMuse on X. It sure looks like playing alongside a legitimate floor general in Fred VanVleet is making Sengun’s life easier. He can catch the ball along the high post instead of having to go through hoops just to get the ball in good post position, and the burden to organize the offense no longer falls solely on his shoulders. Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) It’s not a coincidence at all that Sengun’s biggest scoring performances of the season have come with VanVleet on the active roster. When VanVleet was out due to load management during their first matchup against the Hawks back on Saturday, Sengun scored just 17 points — his lowest tally of the season thus far. Everything is humming for the Rockets at the moment, and the clean bill of health for most of the team’s core players is enabling this level of play from Sengun. On the season, he is averaging 24.5 points, 9.0 rebounds, 7.0 assists, and 1.8 steals on 58/66/77 shooting splits. The Rockets will look to make it five wins in a row on Wednesday when they take on the Milwaukee Bucks on the road at 8:00 PM E.T. item.title: Dream's Angel Reese and her coach blast officiating in WNBA Finals: ‘Just ridiculous'
item.description: Atlanta Dream forward Angel Reese (5) reacts to a foul call during Game 5 of the WNBA Finals against the Golden State Valkyries at Chase Center on Monday. (Yalonda M. James/S.F. Chronicle) The Atlanta Dream have taken 52 more free throws than the Golden State Valkyries through the first five games of the WNBA Finals. The count 130-78 in the Dream's favor. The Dream's 14 free-throw attempts in the Valkyries' 64-55 win at Chase Center in Game 5 on Monday night are the fewest trips to the line Atlanta has had in any game all series. Given the game's physicality, Dream star Angel Reese called out the officiating and her head coach, Karl Smesko, backed her up. "I'm still trying to figure out how to play through the physicality," Reese said. "A lot of us are getting fouled and they're not calling it. Or we're talking to the ref after and they're saying, ‘Oh, we'll get you next time.' So it is a little frustrating, especially in the moment of it. "I mean, I'm kind of used to it because this is happening throughout the season. So I have to just continue to play through it. But honestly, for my teammates, when they're getting slapped to the ground or goggles knocked off, it is frustrating trying to keep them in and keep them confident. We'll figure it out, we'll just have to continue to push through the physicality and hopefully it goes our way the next game." Reese was likely referencing a non-call when the Valkyries' Kiah Stokes and Veronica Burton jumped to defend a driving Allisha Gray in the paint. Burton's arm came down on Gray's head and her goggles flew off her face as she came crashing down. There was no whistle. Reese said she noticed a shift in officiating when the Dream took a 2-1 series lead last week and noted a time in Game 4 that Golden State's Gabby Williams tugged on Reese's arm and the referees didn't blow the whistle. "I want to have Angel's back here. The contact they allow on Angel compared to everybody else is just ridiculous, just ridiculous," Smesko said. "We should have gone to the foul line six to eight more times just on that. Then to miss double-dribbles and travels. Multiple that always led to points. You can't be at this level and make that many mistakes. "There's things that are on us - we're missing shots we should make - but at the same time, it needs to be a whole lot better than it was. It's time that if you push somebody with two hands as they drive, it's got to be a foul and I'm tired of some of the excuses I'm hearing." A best-of-seven series is bound to get increasingly physical as the stakes get higher and teams grow more familiar, and Game 5 fit the bill with collisions, elbows to the face and hard contact on both ends. Reese was whistled for four fouls Monday. She was visibly frustrated when she ran through guard Tiffany Hayes , who was trying to stop her in transition, and was called for an offensive foul. item.title: London City Lionesses new star Alexia Putellas makes history by winning record-equalling third Ballon d'Or Feminin trophy
item.description: TOPSHOT-FBL-AWARD-BALLON D'OR-2026 - AFP Spain icon Alexia Putellas has officially reclaimed her throne at the top of world football by securing a record-equalling third Ballon d'Or Feminin. The midfielder’s triumph ensures the prestigious award remains in Spanish hands for the sixth year in a row, following her heroics for Barcelona and the national team. Spanish dominance continues at the top Putellas has once again been crowned the finest player in the women's game, collecting the 2026 Ballon d'Or Feminin. The 32-year-old midfielder, often referred to as 'La Reina', has now matched the record of three titles held by her international team-mate Aitana Bonmati. This victory marks a significant milestone for Spanish football, as Putellas and Bonmati have shared the last six awards between them, dating back to Putellas' first win in 2021. The voting process saw Putellas emerge as the clear winner following an international poll of journalists from Fifa's top-50 nations. She beat out former Barcelona team-mate Ewa Pajor, who finished in second place, while Manchester City's prolific forward Khadija Shaw took third. The victory is particularly sweet for Putellas, who has successfully navigated the long road back from a devastating ACL injury suffered just before the European Championships in 2022. An emotional victory speech Accepting the trophy on stage, Putellas delivered a moving speech that reflected on her difficult journey back from injury. She highlighted her former teammates and staff shared resilience through difficult times. "We lived incredible moments as a team, we overcame certain difficulties in the form of injuries. It was a pride to be captain of all of you," she said. The midfielder also took a moment to acknowledge her personal support system, which helped her through the darkest days of her recovery process. "It is a trophy for my work, but these people who have family, mother, sister, friends, all my team off the field, that we have known each other for a long time. I am aware that if during last season I enjoyed myself again as I did, it is thanks to you. I remember when my leg failed, the pains in my knee, when I learned to walk and run again, and when I had the most doubts, you were there," she added emotionally. Unrivalled statistics in a quadruple season The midfielder's victory was backed by a sensational individual campaign where she registered 21 goals and 13 assists across all competitions. While Barcelona secured a historic quadruple, Putellas took on extra responsibility in the absence of the injured Bonmati, who missed five months of the season. Her creative output was unmatched, as she completed more passes into the final third and created more chances than any other player across the major European leagues. In the Champions League specifically, Putellas netted seven goals as the Catalan giants secured their fourth continental crown in six years. item.title: The good and bad of Sunday’s outdoor NHL game — and what Utah can learn from it
item.description: The Winnipeg Jets enter the stadium for a hockey game against the Montreal Canadiens in the NHL Heritage Classic in Winnipeg, Manitoba, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (Fred Greenslade/The Canadian Press via AP) | Fred Greenslade The first of three outdoor NHL games on the 2026–27 calendar happened Sunday, with the Winnipeg Jets hosting the Montreal Canadiens. The next one will take place at Rice-Eccles Stadium in Salt Lake City. Here’s what went well at Princess Auto Stadium, as well as the things the league can learn for the New Year’s Eve matchup between the Utah Mammoth and the Colorado Avalanche. What went well at the 2026 Heritage Classic? Nostalgia With “heritage” in the name of the event, nostalgia is a major focus of the marquee Canadian outdoor games. That was at the root of many stylistic decisions in Winnipeg. The border around the arena was made to look like a cozy log cabin, right down to the roaring fireplace and the framed pictures on the walls for a rustic feel. A Canadian flag is unfurled before the NHL Heritage Classic hockey game between the Winnipeg Jets and the Montreal Canadiens in Winnipeg, Manitoba, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (Fred Greenslade/The Canadian Press via AP) | Fred Greenslade The pregame performers included a folk band and “The Asham Stompers,” who blended Indigenous dance with square dancing. Both teams’ jerseys were nods to the past. The Jets reused their 2016 Heritage Classic jerseys, which are based on the “Jets 1.0″ jerseys from before the team migrated to Arizona in 1996. The Canadiens have more or less used the same jerseys since they joined the NHL in 1917, but their Heritage Classic jerseys used a logo and cream color that more closely resembles the original design. They also added a number of fine details to acknowledge the past. Perhaps the most nostalgia, however, came from the alumni game — especially on the Jets’ side, where past greats like Blake Wheeler, Andrew Ladd, Bryan Little and, for the first time since his sudden retirement, fan favorite Dustin Byfuglien were present. “The way our chapter in Winnipeg ended wasn’t how any of us imagined it would,” Byfuglien said in a statement released by the Jets Monday evening. “There were a lot of emotions, a lot left unsaid, and a goodbye that never really happened. For years, I’ve carried a little sadness about that. Not because of the hockey, but because of the people.” He was met with a warm ovation when he participated in the ceremonial faceoff ahead of the big game. Winnipeg loves you, Dustin Byfuglien 💙 pic.twitter.com/q6t8H2p7Qp — Sportsnet (@Sportsnet) October 25, 2026 Nostalgia probably won’t play as big of a role in Utah’s outdoor game, simply because the team doesn’t have nearly as rich of a history as the Canadiens or Jets. They don’t have enough retired alumni to form a line, let alone an entire alumni game. item.description: Photo by Jonathan Bachman/Getty Images Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream find themselves down 3-2 in the WNBA Finals, and they believe the recent shift in officiating has a lot to do with their predicament. At one point, the Dream looked to be comfortably en route to their first WNBA championship, having taken a 2-1 lead over the Golden State Valkyries. However, the Dream lost their next two games consecutively and are now just one more loss away from having their WNBA Finals dream turn into a nightmare. Angel Reese suggests referees ‘shifted’ against Atlanta Dream after Game 3 Speaking to reporters after their loss in Game 5 of the WNBA Finals, Angel Reese pointed out how frustrated she and her teammates have been with the unfair foul calls they’ve received She suggested that the officials had been making calls in favour of the Valkyries, and that had been the case since Game 3, when the Dream took a 2-1 lead in the series. Reese said: “I would definitely say last game, for sure. There was also a possession where Gabby pulled me on purpose, and she was screaming, ‘foul, foul, foul,’ and they didn’t call it. So that definitely was frustrating for sure. “And her team is saying it, and they’re all screaming foul, but the refs – I don’t know what’s going on – why they can’t hear it? “And I know I have the mismatch, especially since we were talking about matchups. So when I do switch on the post, and I’m a lot stronger than the opponent, I should be able to turn, and they’re calling an offensive foul, but I’m getting pushed before that. So that is frustrating for sure. “It definitely shifted when we went up 2-1. Things shifted, and I don’t know what happened, but it definitely took a big turn.” While the officiating can be questioned by the players, Reese and her teammates must also take accountability for their poor performances. Across the last two games, Reese’s numbers have been quite poor, as she has averaged just 7.5 points, 12.0 rebounds, 4.0 assists, 0.5 steals, and 1.5 blocks while shooting 20.0% from the field. In fact, Reese has just made four of her last 20 field goal attempts in Games 4 and 5, showing how well the defensive schemes the Valkyries have used on her have worked. item.title: Where are Wales internationals really made?
item.description: Dewi Lake, Adam Beard and Jac Morgan all now ply their trade outside Wales [Getty Images] Born in Wales, educated in one region, polished in another and given a professional debut somewhere else. The journey to a Wales jersey is rarely as straightforward as the badge on a player's shirt. Where does a Wales international come from? For most, the answer is Wales. But that only tells a fraction of the story. BBC Sport has traced the past 100 men to make their Wales debuts - from where they were born, through junior clubs and schools, into academies, first professional appearances and the clubs they represent today. It is a journey that starts on local playing fields, crosses the Severn Bridge and sometimes stretches halfway around the world. And with the future shape of Welsh professional rugby under scrutiny, it helps explain who does what in producing an international. The research divides each player's journey into five stages. Some classifications require judgement where pathways overlap; our full approach is explained in the methodology at the end of this article. Where were they born? Of the past 100 Wales debutants, 76 were born in Wales, 17 in England and seven elsewhere. That overseas group includes New Zealand-born Hadleigh Parkes and Johnny McNicholl, as well as Bradley Roberts, who was born in South Africa. Their birth certificates tell you very little about where they became professional rugby players. Equally, being born in Wales does not mean a player stayed there. Louis Rees-Zammit and Dafydd Jenkins are two examples of Welsh-born talent whose route to the senior game led them across the border. The more revealing question is what happened after those players first picked up a rugby ball. Where did they learn the game? For 78 of the 100, their formative rugby education - up to age 16 - was in Wales. We looked at schools, junior clubs and the areas in which players grew up playing, rather than attributing a child's development to whichever professional academy eventually signed him. Cardiff's catchment accounts for 30 of the players, followed by the Ospreys area with 20, Scarlets with 17, Dragons with 10 and North Wales with one. These are not 30 Cardiff academy graduates or 20 Ospreys academy graduates. They are players who learned their rugby in those geographical areas, often thanks to volunteers, teachers and local clubs. Rees-Zammit is a useful illustration. His early rugby was in the Cardiff area, but his pathway would take him to Gloucester. Tommy Reffell developed in the Ospreys area before Leicester Tigers became the next stop on his journey. For both, the Welsh rugby education came first. The professional breakthrough came elsewhere. The fallout from the trade has been intense, especially with the Celtics’ history with the 76ers and subsequent tensions between Brown and former teammate Jayson Tatum. Brian Scalabrine’s claim about Jaylen Brown demanding a trade refuted Scalabrine recently reported that Brown demanded a trade with the front office before he was moved in the summer, something that Brown has fervently denied to ESPN through his PR team. “A representative from Jaylen Brown’s team told ESPN that reports that he demanded a trade or presented the Celtics with a list of demands are “10000% a lie.” Brown never requested a trade to Milwaukee, the representative said. After the deal fell through and Boston informed him he’d be traded, his only request was to have input on his destination.” Brown was hoping to retire as a Celtics legend after winning NBA Finals MVP with the franchise in their 2024 title win, but ultimately lost out to Jayson Tatum in their near-decade-long competition of being the team’s No. 1 option. The bad feelings that have lingered since Brown was traded are clear to see, with Brown himself bringing it up often in the media. item.title: Did Deandre Ayton Play Tonight? Why Wizards’ Center Scored 0 Points
item.description: WASHINGTON, DC - SEPTEMBER 28: Deandre Ayton #8 of the Washington Wizards poses for a portrait during Media Day at CareFirst Arena on September 28, 2026 in Washington, DC. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images). Getty Deandre Ayton has a ton of name value. He’s a former No. 1 overall pick and has spent time for a marquee franchise, the Los Angeles Lakers. These days, though, his on-court value may not be as high as that of his name. Ayton plays for the Washington Wizards now, and if you weren’t paying much attention on Monday night, you might not even have noticed. Did Deandre Ayton Play Tonight? Yes, Ayton was on the floor for the Wizards on Monday night in a 110-103 loss to the Charlotte Hornets . He just struggled to make an impact. Ayton didn’t score a single point. Deandre Ayton Stats Ayton hasn’t been starting for the Wizards, and that remained true on Monday. It severely limits his opportunities. On Monday, for example, Ayton got just 12 minutes of action. In those dozen minutes, Ayton attempted just one field goal, and missed it. He didn’t get to the foul line. Ayton added four rebounds, two assists and one turnover. This was Ayton’s quietest game of the season, but he hasn’t done a ton so far. He got 15 minutes and did score 11 points in the opener. He then had 14 minutes with four points and six rebounds in game two. In game three, Ayton got 16 minutes and scored six points with five rebounds. This was by far Ayton’s poorest showing, but he didn’t look to assert himself while seeing just 12 minutes. It was never going to be a big night for him with that role. Why Deandre Ayton Isn’t Playing More This simply isn’t a spot that Ayton will get more time when everyone is healthy. The Wizards start Alex Sarr and Anthony Davis , two guys who could be starting centers. Davis had 29 points and 10 rebounds on Monday, and Sarr had 12 points, six rebounds and two blocks. Davis does have a long injury history, so that’s part of what makes Ayton’s presence smart. He can also help serve as a mentor for the former No. 2 overall pick Sarr. item.title: Sunderland in Europe: Why We Should Savour Every Away Day
item.description: While things are far from rosy in the garden at SAFC (some would argue that the garden is currently on fire), I’ve found our ongoing and so far successful Europa League campaign to be a rather comforting distraction rather than a detriment. Many a Premier League side over the years has been insipid in the league, but as soon as they enter a Schengen Zone country, they suddenly remember that they are, in fact, competent professional footballers. The financial gulf between England and the rest of Europe is quite frankly ridiculous, so it’s hardly surprising, but our domestic woes shouldn’t detract too much from our promising start in the Europa League. Our opponents for this trip were a classic European name and a powerhouse domestically, but they had struggled in their opening two fixtures, shipping a total of eight goals against Palace and Bayer Leverkusen. Those are two of the toughest opponents they could’ve faced, however, so it was crucial not to underestimate the home side and their fearsome support. While Leiria was an incredible experience, it felt more like pre-season dialled up to 11, and it seems unlikely that it will be a typical example of our European adventures. Our fans basically had the run of the city, the police were beyond lenient, and we could bask in glorious mid-October sunshine. This time around, we braced ourselves for long queues for ticket collection, hostile Polish ultras goading us in the rain, and mandatory coach travel. In short, all the hallmarks of a real European away day. Bring it on. Despite what sounded like a reasonable flight time of 8am, there were still insufficient public transport options to get us to Luton Airport in time, so our group was forced into an overnight stay at the airport’s Premier Inn. I have nothing against the purple budget hotel giant; in fact, they’ve proved a reliable away-day companion over the years, but I did find it hilarious when an automated “Here are the top ten things to do in Luton” email dropped into my inbox. Read the room, people. Still, at least it meant an extra hour or so in bed and made the overpriced but mandatory airport breakfast pint taste a bit less brutal. There were plenty of bleary-eyed fans in red and white gearing up for another exciting but draining away day, and after we touched down in Poznań and eventually made it through the lengthy queue at border control, thanks to the misnamed Entry/Exit System, it was time for a taxi to the city that would be our base for two nights. item.title: Chris Rigg: Sunderland’s Latest Centurion
item.description: POZNAN, POLAND - OCTOBER 22: Chris Rigg of Sunderland AFC controls the ball during the UEFA Europa League 2026/27 League Phase MD3 match between KKS Lech Poznan and Sunderland AFC at Poznan Stadium on October 22, 2026 in Poznan, Poland. (Photo by Tomasz Karczewski/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty Images) | Getty Images It might sound faintly ridiculous given his tender age, youthful looks and his relative lack of experience in the top flight, but in some ways, Chris Rigg is already something of a Sunderland veteran. In early 2027, four eventful and transformative years will have passed since the homegrown prodigy made his first appearence in red and white at first team level, and in the intervening period, he’s become a mainstay as we’ve endured setbacks, punishing lows and unforgettable highs. Rigg made his debut when Tony Mowbray was in the dugout and a carefree Sunderland team was making its way through the Championship. Fast forward to 2026 and he’s graduated to the Régis Le Bris school of Premier League football, and he’s done it without missing a beat and rising to every challenge he’s been set. Like Luke O’Nien and Trai Hume — fixtures in red and white since the club’s final months in League One and even further back than that in O’Nien’s case — Rigg has established himself as a tenacious, reliable and exceptionally exciting player. That backheeled winner against Middlesbrough may be two years previous, but it was at that stage that we began to get a better sense of what he’s all about. On Sunday, Rigg racked up his one hundredth first team appearance for the Lads — and duly marked the occasion with a typically tenacious display during Sunderland’s scrappy home draw with Leeds. Rigg mightn’t be a winger by trade and his chances of a sustained run in the middle may be slim at this stage thanks to the presence of the likes of Enzo Le Fée, but that doesn’t seem to faze him. A hard worker with talent to burn, he was quite possibly one of our most solid performers on Sunday and that sits nicely alongside his efforts in the Europa League. Rigg’s rise to prominence is one of the fruits of his own labours. It’s also a product of his willingness to listen, learn and improve, as well as Kristjaan Speakman’s (a figure I actually happen to think we miss at Sunderland in some respects) long-held belief that showing faith in Cleadon’s talented youngsters would eventually pay dividends. Promotion-winning captain Dan Neil may have left for Rangers, but Rigg remains — a player very much of the here and now, and hopefully a tremendous talent of the future, too. I’ve long believed that local players that graduate to the Sunderland first team are judged by different standards to those that come from far and wide to play for our club. As lads that in many cases grew up watching and experiencing the highs and lows of following the club, they’re living all of our dreams and enjoying the kinds of lifestyles that we ourselves might’ve been fortunate enough to experience

item.description: David Gonzales-Imagn Images Natalie Nakase issues stern reminder to Valkyries after WNBA Finals Game 5 win appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The Golden State Valkyries are just a win away from a historic title after beating the Atlanta Dream, 64-55, in Game 5 of the WNBA Finals at Chase Center on Monday. The Valkyries clamped down on defense , limiting the Dream to only 27% from the field. While it was not pretty, Golden State proved it can gut it out in a low-scoring tussle. However, as coach Natalie Nakase pointed out, it is not the time to celebrate for the Valkyries. Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) “Job’s not done. We did what we’re supposed to. Now we gotta get the next one,” said Nakase. Gabby Williams echoed Nakase’s stern reminder. “Don’t relax! We got another level,” added Williams. “Don't relax.” Natalie Nakase after the Valkyries won Game 5 to take a 3-2 lead in the WNBA Finals 🔥 (via @WNBA ) pic.twitter.com/W0A9zS09Q6 — ClutchPoints (@ClutchPoints) October 27, 2026 Veronica Burton had 13 points, eight rebounds, three assists, and four blocks, while Kiah Stokes added 13 points, eight rebounds, and three blocks. Tiffany Hayes contributed 12 points, three assists, and two steals. The Valkyries have a strong chance to capture their first championship in only their second year in the league. Nakase is fully aware of how important it is to stay balanced, physically and mentally, in a close-out game. She won two rings with the Las Vegas Aces as an assistant coach. Last year, many questioned the Valkyries’ decision to hire Nakase due to her size and background. Many felt she was not ready to call the shots and lead an expansion team. But clearly, she has proven them wrong. She has created an inspiring culture in Golden State, with players willing to run through a wall for her. The Valkyries will look to finish off the Dream in Game 6 at State Farm Arena on Thursday.
